accepted.label: Definition and everyday examples of heuristics
accepted.description: Heuristics are mental shortcuts or rules of thumb developed from past experiences that enable quick decisions, sacrificing optimality for speed. Everyday examples include choosing default outfits or ordering familiar food.
coverage_criteria: Define heuristic and provide an everyday example.
Explain why heuristics prioritize speed over perfection.
accepted.merge_rationale: c29_pro_thinking_001 and c31_pro_thinking_001 both define heuristics as mental shortcuts; c29_pro_thinking_002 provides concrete everyday illustrations, completing a teachable unit on what heuristics are and how they appear in daily life.

accepted.label: Over-reliance on heuristics in political views
accepted.description: People may let political identities and heuristics substitute for detailed information, leading to uninformed viewpoints and resistance to opposing opinions.
coverage_criteria: Describe how heuristics can bias political opinions.
Suggest a strategy to mitigate over-reliance on heuristics in politics.

accepted.label: Availability heuristic
accepted.description: The availability heuristic is the tendency to estimate the frequency of an event by how easily examples come to mind, which can distort perceptions, e.g., overestimating violence due to media coverage.
coverage_criteria: Define the availability heuristic.
Explain how the availability heuristic can distort perceptions of crime rates.

accepted.label: Representativeness heuristic
accepted.description: The representativeness heuristic is when people assume an individual case is more representative than it truly is, often ignoring base rates, as illustrated by physicians overestimating disease likelihood after a positive test.
coverage_criteria: Define the representativeness heuristic.
Explain why a positive test for a rare disease does not guarantee having the disease.

accepted.label: Intellectual humility regarding heuristics
accepted.description: Because heuristics can lead to errors, it is important to remain humble, acknowledge uncertainty, and be open to considering opposing views.
coverage_criteria: Explain why intellectual humility is important when using heuristics.

accepted.label: Professional impact of cognitive biases
accepted.description: Cognitive biases influence decision-making in professional domains such as management, medicine, finance, and law, and recognizing them is key to mitigating errors.
coverage_criteria: Name at least two professional fields where cognitive biases impact decisions.
Explain how recognizing biases helps professionals make better decisions.
accepted.merge_rationale: Single candidate; provides a general overview of biases across professions, complementing specific legal examples.

accepted.label: Confirmation bias in judicial evidence evaluation
accepted.description: Judges may favor evidence that confirms pre-existing beliefs while dismissing contradictory information, compromising impartiality.
coverage_criteria: Define confirmation bias and identify a scenario where it affects a judge's decision.

accepted.label: Hindsight bias in legal foreseeability
accepted.description: Hindsight bias leads people to see past events as more predictable than they were, unfairly skewing judgments of foreseeability in court.
coverage_criteria: Explain hindsight bias and describe its effect on evaluating a defendant's actions.

accepted.label: Conjunction fallacy in probability estimates
accepted.description: The conjunction fallacy occurs when a detailed scenario is judged more probable than a simpler one, violating statistical logic and affecting legal evidence interpretation.
coverage_criteria: Describe the conjunction fallacy and provide an example where added detail inflates perceived probability.

accepted.label: Inadmissible evidence bias
accepted.description: Judges and jurors often struggle to disregard evidence ruled inadmissible, leading to biased verdicts despite instructions.
coverage_criteria: Explain the challenge of ignoring inadmissible evidence and give an example.

accepted.label: Sequential ruling bias
accepted.description: When judges make sequential rulings, they tend to favor the status quo and become more conservative, with decisions being more favorable after breaks.
coverage_criteria: Describe the sequential ruling bias and its effect on judicial decision patterns.

accepted.label: Anchoring effect on sentencing
accepted.description: The anchoring effect occurs when an initial numerical value, even if arbitrary, influences subsequent judgments, leading to biased sentencing.
coverage_criteria: Define anchoring and explain how irrelevant anchors can sway a judge's sentence.
